content:
Today we continue our study in Numbers chapter eleven. Israel had already witnessed the judgment at Taberah, where the fire of Yahweh burned among the outer parts of the camp because of their murmuring. Moses prayed, the fire was quenched, and the place was named Taberah, meaning the place of burning. But soon after this warning, another spirit of dissatisfaction rose up in the camp.

Numbers 11:4 says, "And the mixt multitude that was among them fell a lusting: and the children of Israel also wept again, and said, Who shall give us flesh to eat?" The trouble first began among the mixed multitude, also called the foreign rabble or the gathered crowd. These were non-Israelites who had come out of Egypt together with the children of Israel. Exodus 12:38 says, "And a mixed multitude went up also with them." They may have included Egyptians, foreigners, servants, and slaves from other nations who had joined Israel after seeing the great judgments Yahweh brought upon Egypt. They had physically left Egypt, but Egypt had not fully left their hearts. They had joined the journey of Israel, yet they had not developed the same faith in Yahweh's promises. They walked with the people of God, but their desires still remained in the old land.

It is important to understand that Hobab and the Kenites should not be confused with this complaining rabble. Hobab was a Midianite whom Moses invited later, near Sinai, saying, "Come with us, and we will do thee good."
The mixed multitude had already come out of Egypt with Israel. And the Kenites are later presented in Scripture as a separate family who showed kindness to Israel and lived among Judah. These are not the same people.The foreign rabble began to crave meat intensely. Their desire was not a simple request for food, for they already had food. Yahweh was giving them manna every day. But they became dissatisfied with what He had provided, and began to long for the food of Egypt.

And their craving soon spread to the Israelites. Numbers 11:4 says that after the mixed multitude began lusting, "the children of Israel also wept again."

The spirit of dissatisfaction moved through the camp. One group began speaking about Egypt, others listened, and soon the Israelites themselves joined in the complaint. They began to say, "Who shall give us flesh to eat?" Then they remembered the foods they had eaten in Egypt. Numbers 11:5 says,"We remember the fish, which we did eat in Egypt freely; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlick." They remembered six foods; fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic. They spoke as though Egypt had been a place of comfort and abundance. They remembered the taste of the food, but they forgot the pain of slavery. They remembered the fish but forgot the taskmasters. They remembered the vegetables, but forgot the beatings. They remembered what had entered their mouths, but forgot the cries that had come from their hearts while they were slaves.

They said they had eaten fish freely in Egypt. Egypt had the River Nile, its canals and pools, and many sources of fish, so fish was common and may have been inexpensive. It is also possible that slaves and labourers received fish as part of their food ration, so they may not have paid money directly for it.
But although the fish may have seemed free, their life in Egypt was not free. They may not have paid for the fish with money, but they paid for their life in Egypt with slavery, hard labour, suffering, and oppression. This shows us how sinful desire can change the memory. It makes the old bondage look attractive, and makes the present blessing look worthless. Numbers 11:6 says, "But now our soul is dried away: there is nothing at all, beside this manna, before our eyes." Manna was no ordinary food. It was Yahweh's miraculous provision.It came down from heaven and sustained the whole nation every single day in the wilderness. Yet the people spoke of it as though it were nothing. They said, "There is nothing at all, beside this manna." They were not starving. They were not without food. Their problem was that they no longer valued what Yahweh had given them. They wanted something different, and their desire had become stronger than their gratitude.

Their craving grew so great that they wept openly throughout the camp. Numbers 11:10 says that Moses heard the people weeping in their families, every man at the door of his tent. The complaint had now spread from the mixed multitude to the whole camp. What began as the desire of a few had become the weeping of many families. Yahweh heard their complaint and told Moses that He would give them meat. But He made it clear that this was not a reward for their faith. It was a response to their rejection of Him. Numbers 11:18 says, "Sanctify yourselves against to morrow, and ye shall eat flesh." Yahweh told them that they would not eat meat for only one day, or two, or five, or ten, or twenty days. He said they would eat it for a whole month, until it came out of their nostrils and became disgusting to them. The meaning was that they had demanded meat so strongly that Yahweh would give them an overwhelming abundance of the very thing they craved.

Before this happened, Yahweh instructed Moses to gather seventy elders, and He placed upon them some of the spirit that was upon Moses, so that they could help him carry the heavy burden of the people. Then Yahweh sent a wind. Numbers 11:31 says, "And there went forth a wind from Yahweh, and brought quails from the sea, and let them fall by the camp." The wind carried an enormous number of quail toward the camp. The birds covered the area around Israel, reaching about a day's journey on every side of the camp, and they flew about two cubits above the ground, making them easy to catch. The people immediately went out to gather them. Numbers 11:32 says, "And the people stood up all that day, and all that night, and all the next day, and they gathered the quails." They gathered quail through the day, through the night, and through the following day, and then spread them all around the camp, probably to prepare, dry, and preserve the meat. The person who gathered the least gathered ten homers; a very large measure, roughly two thousand litres or more (Approx 900 to 1300 Kilos depending on the weight of the bird).
The passage reveals not only hunger, but greed. They did not gather a small amount for one or two meals. Even the one who gathered the least collected far more than a single household could reasonably eat.

But many of them never lived to enjoy it for a month. Numbers 11:33 says, "And while the flesh was yet between their teeth, ere it was chewed, the wrath of Yahweh was kindled against the people, and Yahweh smote the people with a very great plague." The judgment came suddenly. While the meat was still between their teeth, before they had even finished chewing it, a severe plague struck them. The Bible does not explain the exact medical symptoms. It simply says that Yahweh struck the people with a very great plague. Some have suggested that the quail may have caused a kind of food poisoning, since certain migratory quail can sometimes carry toxins from the plants they eat, and the warm wilderness, improper storage, or contaminated meat may have contributed. The main point is that Yahweh's judgment came upon them.

Even if He used a natural cause, the event was not an accident. The plague came because they despised His provision, longed for Egypt, and gave themselves over to uncontrolled craving.

Numbers 11:34 says, "And he called the name of that place Kibroth-hattaavah: because there they buried the people that lusted." Kibroth-hattaavah means the graves of craving, or the graves of lust, or the graves of those who desired.

The place received its name from what happened there. The people had craved meat. They had wept for meat. They had gathered enormous quantities of meat. But the very place where their craving was satisfied became the place where they were buried. Their desire began in their hearts, passed into their words, spread through the camp, controlled their actions, and finally led them to their graves. They remembered Egypt and despised manna. They rejected the provision of Yahweh and demanded the desires of their flesh. They gathered more than they needed. And in the end, their greed became their graves.The lessons for the New Creation from the mixed multitude, the manna, the quail, and Kibroth-hattaavah are very deep. God willing, we will study those lessons in tomorrow's Morning Light.

title: Prayer
text:
O Yahweh, our God,

We tremble at how quickly a craving can grow into a grave.

Guard our hearts from longing after the old life we were delivered from,

and from despising the daily bread You so faithfully provide.

Forgive us when our desire grows stronger than our gratitude.

Teach us to be content with what You give, and to remember the cost of Egypt,

lest we remember its taste and forget its chains.

Keep us from the greed that gathers more than we need and loses its soul in the gathering.

"Keep back Your servant also from presumptuous sins; let them not have dominion over me." - Psalm 19:13

In the name of Christ, the true bread from heaven, we pray. Amen.
